notes.meaning: Elihu turns directly to Job, calling him by his personal name. Job's three older friends never addressed him by name in all their speeches. Elihu asks Job to give him a full and patient hearing before deciding whether his words are right.

Elihu announces that he is ready to speak after carefully weighing what to say. He compares his words to food tasted on the palate, wanting to make sure that everything he says is wholesome and sound.
Elihu promises that his speech comes from an honest and sincere heart. Unlike the older friends who spoke out of anger or prejudice, Elihu claims he will speak the plain truth without deceit.

Elihu reminds Job that God's Spirit created him and gave him breath, just like Adam at the beginning. Because Elihu is an ordinary human being made by God, he can discuss these deep matters with Job on equal ground.
Elihu invites Job to answer him and organize his defense like a legal case. He offers Job complete freedom to stand up and push back once he has heard what Elihu has to say.

Elihu points out that he is only a fellow creature shaped from clay, standing before God just like Job. Job had wished for an arbiter who would not overwhelm him with divine glory, and Elihu steps forward as a fellow human to fill that role.
Elihu assures Job that he has no reason to fear him. Because Elihu is not God, his presence will not terrify Job, nor will he use harsh force or cruelty against him.
Elihu explains that he is answering things he heard Job speak with his own ears. He wants Job to know that his criticism rests on Job's actual statements, not on second-hand rumors.

Elihu quotes Job as claiming to be completely pure, innocent, and free from all sin. While Job had firmly defended his general integrity against false charges of secret crimes, he had never actually claimed to be sinless.

differ.view: Some read Job's claims of purity in light of Christ's imputed righteousness, where a believer is counted completely clean before God through faith.

notes.meaning: Elihu points out Job's complaint that God was looking for excuses to attack him and treating him like an enemy. In his terrible suffering, Job had felt that God had turned against him without any good reason.
Elihu recalls Job's words that God had locked his feet in stocks and kept watch over every move he made. Job had felt trapped and guarded like a criminal who had broken the law.

Elihu tells Job that he is wrong to talk this way because God is far greater than any human being. Since God possesses supreme wisdom, justice, and power, humans have no right to question His motives or put Him on trial.

Elihu asks why Job complains that God does not answer every question a person asks. As the sovereign ruler of the universe, God is not required to explain the secret reasons behind all of His actions to human beings.

Elihu explains that God does speak to people in different ways, even when humans fail to notice or understand His voice. God actively reaches out to teach and guide, but people often miss what He is doing.

Elihu describes the first way God speaks, which is through dreams and visions of the night during deep sleep. When daily business is quieted and the body rests, the human mind is open to receive divine warnings.

differ.view: God still actively speaks to believers today through revelatory dreams and night visions.

notes.meaning: In those dreams, God opens people's spiritual ears and seals His instruction into their hearts. He imprints His warnings deeply so they will remember the lesson and take it to heart when they wake up.

God sends these warnings to turn a person away from evil actions and to keep him from becoming proud. His purpose is to protect people from their own destructive impulses before they fall into deeper trouble.

differ.view: Suffering and divine warnings are gracious discipline designed to uncover and purge the hidden pride that remains even in godly people.

notes.meaning: By turning a person back from sin, God keeps his soul from the Pit, which means the grave or destruction. God's warnings rescue people from dying before their time or perishing by sudden violence.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The phrase translated 'perishing by the sword' can also be read as crossing the river of death that leads into the underworld.

notes.meaning: Elihu introduces God's second way of speaking, which is through bodily sickness and deep physical pain. God uses the misery of a sickbed as a loving discipline to get a person's attention and lead him to repentance.
The sick person becomes so ill that he loses all desire for food and even detests the finest meals. Severe suffering strips away the normal pleasures of life and humbles the sufferer.

The person's flesh wastes away from sight until only skin and bones are left, and bones that were once hidden now stick out. Elihu describes an emaciated condition that closely mirrors Job's own physical agony.
The suffering person comes to the very brink of the grave, and his life approaches the agents of death. He is at the point where human doctors and friends have given up all hope of recovery.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The messengers of death may refer to ancient cultural beliefs about death-dealing spirits or poetic personifications of the grave.

notes.meaning: Elihu presents the hope of a messenger or mediator, one out of a thousand, who can step in on behalf of the sufferer. This messenger teaches the person what is right, explaining that God's discipline is just and pointing him toward repentance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The mediator is likely an angelic figure in God's heavenly court pleading for the sufferer, rather than a human teacher.

notes.meaning: God shows mercy to the dying person and commands that he be spared from the pit of death because a ransom has been found. Christian commentators have traditionally seen this ransom fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who offered His life to deliver sinners from eternal death.
Once the person is pardoned and spared, his physical body begins to recover until his skin is as fresh as a child's. His strength returns, and he enters a new season of health and vigor.
The restored person prays to God and receives His favor. He enters God's presence with joy, and God treats him as fully reconciled and righteous.

The healed man confesses publicly before others that he had sinned and twisted what was right, yet God did not give him the punishment he deserved. True restoration leads to honest confession and praise for God's mercy.
The grateful man continues his praise, declaring that God redeemed his soul from the pit of death so he can walk in the light. God has turned back judgment and granted him a second chance at life.

Elihu summarizes that God repeatedly does all these things for people, reaching out two or three times to save them. God is remarkably patient, using warnings, trials, and mediators to turn sinners back to Himself.
The main purpose of God's discipline is to bring a person back from the edge of death so he may enjoy the light of life. God's ultimate desire is to heal and restore, not to destroy.
Elihu urges Job to pay close attention and stay silent while he continues to explain his case. He wants Job to reflect carefully on these truths instead of reacting too quickly.

Elihu invites Job to speak if he has any genuine objection, saying he would gladly vindicate Job if possible. Unlike the older friends who wanted to prove Job guilty, Elihu claims he desires to see Job cleared if the truth allows it.
Elihu finishes by saying that if Job has no response, he should remain quiet and listen so Elihu can teach him true wisdom. Because Job offers no reply, Elihu prepares to continue his speech.
